metric.dependency_simplicity.method: Static inspection of provided C++ micro (mb00-mb11) and adversarial (ADV-*) benchmark programs under template/programs/cpp/micro and template/programs/cpp/adversarial.
observations: All inspected programs (e.g. mb01.cpp) depend only on the C++ standard library headers: <chrono>, <cstdint>, <cstdio>, <cstdlib>, <cstring>.
No third-party package manager (vcpkg, conan) or external native library dependency is referenced in any sampled source file.

C++'s dependency model is intrinsically simple for single-translation-unit workloads: no build-system manifest, lockfile, or package registry is mandatory to compile and run a program (a single 'c++ -O2 file.cpp -o out' suffices).

However, C++ has no standardized, built-in package/dependency manager as a language feature (unlike e.g. Cargo for Rust or Go modules); beyond header-only or single-file use, dependency management is delegated to external tooling (CMake + vcpkg/Conan/FetchContent), which is a language-design limitation rather than an ecosystem-maturity one because the language specification itself defines no module/dependency resolution mechanism (C++20 modules improve compilation units but not dependency acquisition).

Score reflects: very high simplicity for the actual workloads evaluated (zero external deps, trivial single-command build) offset by the intrinsic lack of a language-defined dependency/package mechanism, a durable language-level property distinct from package-manager maturity (which belongs to Ecosystem).
metric.dependency_simplicity.score_rationale: 78/100: excellent for the sampled zero-dependency workloads; deduction for lacking a standardized in-language dependency-resolution mechanism.

metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.method: Static inspection of standard headers and constructs used across sampled micro/adversarial C++ programs; review of ISO C++ language design properties relevant to platform neutrality.
observations: Sampled programs use only ISO-standard headers (<chrono>, <cstdio>, <cstdlib>, <cstring>, <cstdint>) with no platform-specific APIs (no POSIX headers, no Windows.h, no inline assembly, no compiler builtins) in the inspected files.

C++ as a language is defined by an ISO standard implemented by multiple independent compilers (GCC, Clang, MSVC) across all major OS/architecture combinations, a strong intrinsic platform-neutrality property.

However, C++ has portability weaknesses baked into the language semantics itself: implementation-defined and undefined behavior for integer overflow, pointer arithmetic, type punning, struct layout/padding, and sizeof/endianness are not fully specified by the standard, so strictly-portable code requires more care than higher-level languages (Java, Go, Rust) require.

No OS-specific syscalls, filesystem path separators, or ABI-specific behavior were observed in the inspected workload sources, indicating the benchmark authors wrote genuinely platform-neutral C++ using only standard-library facilities.

The absence of a mandated stable ABI across compiler versions (a language design property, not a tooling one) further constrains binary-level portability, though source-level portability of standard C++ remains strong.
metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.score_rationale: 72/100: strong source-level cross-platform standard-library design offset by language-level portability caveats (UB/implementation-defined behavior, no stable ABI) intrinsic to the C++ language specification.
